stem: Which instruction best reduces choking risk when feeding a toddler?

options.A: Offer hard candy and whole nuts as routine snacks because these foods help strengthen chewing skills.
options.B: Serve whole grapes and round hot-dog slices because chewing is mature enough once a toddler can walk.
options.C: Allow the child to eat while walking or playing because movement does not meaningfully affect choking risk.
options.D: Prepare foods in developmentally appropriate shapes, sizes, and textures, avoid small hard or round hazards, and have the child sit while eating under close supervision.

rationale: CDC choking-prevention guidance recommends preparing food in a shape, size, and texture appropriate for the child's development; avoiding small, sticky, or hard foods; having the child sit while eating rather than walk or crawl; and supervising the child at all times during meals. Whole grapes, hot dogs/sausages, whole or chopped nuts, and hard candy are listed as potential choking hazards. D combines the supported prevention measures; A through C increase risk.
educational_objective: Teach caregivers to reduce toddler choking risk through developmentally appropriate food preparation, avoidance of common choking hazards, seated eating, and direct supervision.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Choking Hazards — Infant and Toddler Nutrition
source_locator: Choking prevention — Foods and preparation; Meals and snacktime; Always; Potential choking hazards for young children
source_claim_supported: CDC recommends developmentally appropriate food shape/size/texture, avoiding small hard choking hazards, seated eating, and continuous supervision; whole grapes, hot dogs, nuts, and hard candy are listed choking hazards.

source_original.stem: Which instruction best reduces choking risk when feeding a toddler?

options.A: Offer hard candy and whole nuts as routine snacks because these foods strengthen chewing skills
options.B: Serve whole grapes and round hot-dog slices because chewing ability is mature once a toddler walks
options.C: Allow eating while walking or playing because movement does not meaningfully change choking risk
options.D: Prepare foods in developmentally safe shapes and sizes and avoid small, hard, round choking hazards

source_original.rationale: CDC recommends preparing food to an age-appropriate size, shape, and texture, avoiding small/hard foods, cutting spherical foods such as grapes into small pieces, and supervising children while eating.
source_original.source_detail: Infant and Toddler Nutrition, Choking Prevention and Potential Choking Hazards; March 11, 2026; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Kept the correct CDC construct but strengthened D with seated eating and direct supervision, aligned every distractor to specific CDC-listed hazards/behaviors, and verified the NCSBN 2026 safety blueprint at printed p.8.

audit_findings.source_authority: CDC 2026 choking guidance; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.claim_audit: CDC directly supports food-preparation, seated-eating, supervision, and hazard claims in the final item.

distractor_audit.A: Hard candy and whole/chopped nuts are listed choking hazards.
distractor_audit.B: Uncut grapes and hot dogs/sausages are listed choking hazards; walking does not establish safe chewing.
distractor_audit.C: CDC says the child should sit while eating and not crawl or walk.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D reduces risk across food preparation and mealtime behavior.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are caregiver feeding instructions; no grammatical or format cue determines the answer.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN printed p.8 explicitly includes protecting clients from injury and safety education.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read CDC March 2026 guidance and NCSBN p.8, challenged each food/behavior claim, and confirmed D remained uniquely correct.
